content:
Since \(a+b+c\) is prime, none of \(a,b,c\) can be prime: if one were a prime \(p\), then pairwise gcd conditions force \(p\) to divide the other two, making the whole sum divisible by \(p\). Thus all three are composite.

Also, since the sum is prime and greater than \(2\), it is odd. So either all three numbers are odd, or exactly one is odd and two are even.

- If all three are odd composites, each is at least \(9\), so the sum is at least \(27\). The only prime below \(31\) possible would be \(29\), but \(29=9+9+11\), and \(11\) is prime, impossible.

- If exactly one is odd, call it \(x\). The two even numbers must each share an odd prime factor with \(x\), so each is at least \(6\). For a sum below \(31\), this gives \(x<31-12=19\), so \(x=9\) or \(15\).
  - If \(x=9\), both evens must be multiples of \(6\), so the total sum is divisible by \(3\), not prime.
  - If \(x=15\), each even must be a multiple of \(6\) or \(10\). For a prime sum below \(31\), the two evens would need to sum to \(2,4,8,\) or \(14\). The smallest possible sum is \(6+6=12\), and \(14\) cannot be formed from multiples of \(6\) or \(10\). So no such prime below \(31\).

Thus no prime sum below \(31\) works. But \(6,10,15\) have pairwise gcds \(2,3,5\), and
\[
6+10+15=31,
\]
which is prime.

\[
\boxed{31}
\]
